conclusion: Penman and Wells, INTEGERS 13 (2013) A57, Theorem 21, state DeepMind Problem 42's quantity character for character and reach sup g = ln(32/5)/ln(26/5) = 1.125944426, above the AlphaEvolve value, which re-counts exactly to 1.1219357375 on 309 integers. Their Q_36, a 197-element set published thirteen years earlier, already beats it at g = 1.1219505699, so the world_record marking on Problem 42 does not hold for the lower bound on C.
confidence: Lean on it fully for the comparison itself. Every count is exact integer enumeration, the decisive inequality is decided at 120 decimal digits rather than in float, Corollary 13's four counting formulas were reproduced by enumeration at 64 values of j with zero mismatches, and four independent numbers printed in the same paper (g(A_15) = 1.0717, f(X) = ln(51)/ln(47), f(Q_10) = 1.030597781, f-hat(Q_19) = 1.028377107) all recompute exactly, which is what rules out reading the wrong normalisation. The one real hazard, that the paper's abstract quantity f = ln|A+A|/ln|A-A| is a different function that ranks these two sets the other way, was found and is handled explicitly. Two things are NOT verified here and are taken from the issue rather than read: that Staps (2015) records this as best known, and that nothing published between 2013 and now beats it. So the safe statement is 'the 2013 result beats the AlphaEvolve value', not 'the 2013 result is the current record'.
operator_decision_required: Whether anything is said upstream to DeepMind, and if so whether it is a comment on issue #5 (which is AI-produced and unreviewed, and would then carry a second AI-produced confirmation) or an independent report. The brief put posting out of scope, so nothing was posted. Note also that a reply would be confirming a competitor lab's error using a published human paper, which is a positioning question and not a mathematical one.

threads.what: The baseline 1.0598 that AlphaEvolve is reported to have improved on matches nothing printed in the Penman-Wells paper. That paper lists its four families' suprema on the same page as Theorem 21: 1.0867 (T_j, T'_j), 1.0261 (R_j), 1.0592 (M_j). 1.0598 is six units in the fourth decimal off the M_j value.

core_candidates.what: An exact log-ratio comparator: decide g(A1) > g(A2) for integer counts without a float, via high-precision decimal cross-multiplication of the two logarithms (probe.py:g_beats, 12 lines, stdlib only).
core_candidates.why_reusable: Every 'does our construction beat theirs' verdict in this lab reduces to comparing two ratios of logarithms of integers, and reporting a float ratio invites exactly the rounding argument a reader will make when the margin is 1.5e-05, as it is here.
